generation.hypothesis: Replacing scarce and expensive rare‐earth elements in conventional Gd‐based magnetocaloric alloys with a design based on transition metals—specifically by using a high‐entropy alloy composition such as FeCoNiTi—will improve the magnetocaloric effect near room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional magnetocaloric alloy based on rare‐earth elements (e.g., Gd‐based alloys) with narrow temperature windows and high cost.
generation.intervention: Chemical composition change by substituting rare‐earth elements with alternative transition metals (Fe, Co, Ni) augmented by Ti in an equiatomic ratio to form FeCoNiTi.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed near room temperature (around 300 K) under cyclic magnetic field changes.
generation.structural_mediator: The dual-phase microstructure developed via rapid quenching in the high-entropy FeCoNiTi alloy, which exhibits distinct magnetic ordering transitions.
generation.mechanism: Substitution alters the electronic structure and magnetic exchange interactions, potentially shifting the magnetic transition closer to room temperature and increasing the isothermal entropy change, thereby enhancing the magnetocaloric properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: An enhanced magnetocaloric effect characterized by a larger isothermal magnetic entropy change and improved adiabatic temperature change compared to conventional rare‐earth based materials.
generation.baseline: Typical performance metrics of conventional Gd‐based magnetocaloric alloys.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness may depend on the phase fractions and ordering transitions present in the FeCoNiTi alloy, and the improvement is limited to the magnetic behavior near room temperature. Significant enhancement must be observed under external magnetic fields used in refrigeration applications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the enhancement in the magnetocaloric effect is uncertain, as it depends on the detailed microstructural evolution and the balance between different magnetic phases within the alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with a conventional Gd-based magnetocaloric alloy and another with the high-entropy FeCoNiTi alloy. Subject both samples to identical magnetic field cycling near room temperature. Use rapid-quenching processing for the FeCoNiTi alloy to obtain the desired microstructure. Characterize the samples using X-ray diffraction (to confirm phase composition), scanning electron microscopy (for microstructure), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (for composition homogeneity).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy FeCoNiTi sample does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ΔS_m and ΔT_ad relative to the conventional Gd-based alloy under the same conditions, or if the improvements are below expected practical thresholds, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We report the magnetic properties of the as-cast high-entropy alloy (HEA) FeCoNiTi, characterized by a dual phase comprising the face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal C14 Laves phases. The HEA manifests three distinct ferromagnetic orderings at 1084, 214, and 168 K. The emergence of the 214 K transition is attributed to the influence of the C14 phase. The high-temperature ordering at 1084 K is associated with the fcc phase, which exhibits an additional ferromagnetic ordering at 168 K. The coercive field of the fcc phase attains 667 Oe at 400 K. Electronic structure calculations conducted for both phases substantiate the presence of ferromagnetic ground states. Comparative analyses between experimental and theoretical values are undertaken in the context of saturation magnetization. A comprehensive discussion is presented, delving into the origin of the relatively high coercive field observed at high temperatures in the fcc phase.
